“Figure it Out” example 1
In early April 2022, Jorden Backman, one of our FPs, bought two Crumbl stores in Utah.
The Bountiful store was one of the first Crumbl stores; the Centerville store opened February 2021.
Crumbl Centerville is only 3.7 miles away from Bountiful, a 6-minute drive.
The purchase price for both stores was $1.5M, the new owner Jorden Backman and his partner took out an SBA loan with a variable interest rate.
The new owners have been worried about flat sales and even declines from 2021.
They have reached out to you, as their Success Coach, to help them understand:
What's causing this trend? 
How can they effectively boost sales? 
What realistic expectations should they set moving forward?

“Figure it Out” example 2
You are the Success Coach over some stores in Georgia.
These stores are owned by two different Franchise Partners, each of whom owns several stores. 
Two of your stores, Cumming and Lawrenceville, are relatively similar as measured by 2022 sales.
However, one is generating approximately a 15% profit, while the other is generating about 5.0%.
Data you have gathered (sales, profit, profit as percentage of sales):
GA - Cumming	 $ 2,134,852 	 $   107,221 	5.02%	"James Griffin"
GA - Lawrenceville	 $ 2,745,742 	 $   417,785 	15.22%	"Daniel Scott“
Both FPs are looking for insights from you.
What will you do in order to understand 
why
 their profits are so different?
How will you consult and advise each of the FPs?

Decision Trap #1 =  
“Plunging in”
We want to “get going.”
We are impatient with meetings (due to bad experience).
“Furious activity” feels good, and it gets confused with forward motion.
The problem is us! That is, bad habits…
We tend toward one extreme of interaction and integration.
Kiddie soccer
: 
Everyone
 is clumped at the same ball.
Silos
: 
Nobody
 talks to anyone else at key moments.

We have a tendency to jump to the end. 
That is, we:
start with solutions.
start with biases and initial conclusions, i.e., we
backfill justifications and reasoning.
confuse “hunting” vs “fishing.”

Making intentional choices is almost always better than executing a process thoughtlessly – whether by habit, convenience, convention or 
expedience.

Facilitate 
constructive conflict
: focused on tasks & progress.
Exercise 
sequence discipline.
Everything that matters has a “right time” to consider.
We can’t move forward if we try to do everything at once.
Using a deliberate sequence also helps us defuse team conflict and break out of analysis paralysis and other loops of discussion.
Capturing out-of-sequence issues and suggestions ensures that they are addressed at the appropriate time.
It also reassures everyone that their issues are being heard. 
Have the right fight at the right time.

“How many customers have expressed these concerns about the quality of our new product line?”
“Could the root cause be our lack of organizational capabilities in sales force management?”
“Can we go around the table for a second, and see whether anything is unclear, or still of concern?”
“Would it be helpful if I captured any comments about deadline concerns, and organize a list of pain points?”
“Has anyone else been struck by how often people have used the word ‘chaos’ during this meeting?”
“Should we spend a few more minutes getting the objective clear before moving on discussing calendar?”
“What are some examples of these ‘distribution challenges,’ and what boxes might we put them into?”

Simplifying is not so simple.
It’s easier to ramble on than to get to the point.
It’s easier to collect everyone’s words and ideas than to sort out which ones actually matter.
Processing is a quality-assurance step.
Don’t just throw everything into the “group sink.”
Synthesize.
